subject: tech
title: Passwords and Private Info
about: Passwords as secret keys shared only with parents, why long passwords are strong, what counts as private information (full name, address, phone number, school, passwords, photos of your home) and keeping it out of games and websites, asking before signing up, logging out, and the digital footprint. NC K2-NI-02 (passwords and strong passwords), K2-NI-03 (digital footprint and protecting personal information) and K2-IC-04 (responsible login and logoff). Read it together and keep the tone calm: he is never in trouble for asking.
tip: Make up a silly strong password together, like purple frog jumps 9, and talk about why it beats 1234.

cards.note: A password unlocks your account, like a key unlocks a door. Only you and your parents hold it.

cards.q: Who are the only people you share your password with?
cards.note: Your parents keep your password safe with you. Nobody else needs it, not even friends.

cards.q: A friend asks for your password. What do you do?
cards.note: You can say, sorry, passwords are private. Then tell your grown-up that a friend asked.

cards.q: Which password is the hardest for someone to guess?
cards.note: Long passwords made of a few words and a number are hard to guess. Short ones like 1 2 3 4 are easy.

cards.q: Is your own name a good password?
cards.note: Everyone knows your name, so it is easy to guess. Pick words nobody would think of.

cards.q: Why do we use a strong password?
cards.note: A strong password stops other people from getting into your account and your things.

cards.q: Your full name, address and phone number are what kind of information?
cards.note: Private information is about you and your family. It stays with you and your grown-ups.

cards.q: A game asks, what is your name and your school? What do you do?
cards.note: Games and websites do not need to know who you are or where you go to school. Stop and get a grown-up.

cards.q: A website wants your home address to send you a free prize. What do you do?
cards.note: Free prizes online are often tricks to get your private information. Grown-ups know what to do.

cards.q: Is a photo of your house with the house number private information?
cards.note: A photo can show where you live. Ask a grown-up before any photo goes online.

cards.q: A new app says, sign up here! Who do you ask before you make an account?
cards.note: Signing up means giving the app information about you. A grown-up decides if the app is okay.

cards.q: You finish playing on a shared computer. What do you do before you walk away?
cards.note: Logging out closes your account so the next person cannot see your things. Log in again next time.

cards.q: What do you type to get into your own account?
cards.note: Logging in with your password tells the computer it is really you.

cards.q: Things you post or type online can stay there for a long time. What is that called?
cards.note: Like footprints in wet sand, what you do online leaves marks that can stay. Think before you post.

cards.q: A video you post online can be seen by how many people?
cards.note: Once something is online, many people may see it and copy it. That is part of your digital footprint.

cards.q: Where is a safe place to keep passwords?
wrong: on a sign in the yard
cards.note: Your parents can write passwords down in a safe place at home. Never in a game or a message.

cards.q: Which of these is private information?
cards.note: Favorite colors and animals are fine to share. Phone numbers, addresses and passwords are private.
